nature-econ-023.q: How is bounded willpower linked to hyperbolic discounting?
nature-econ-023.a: They are closely linked: hyperbolic discounting is the tendency to value immediate rewards more than future ones.

nature-econ-046.q: Why might having more options not leave people better off?
nature-econ-046.a: Classical economics predicts more options leave people at least as well off, but each option costs time and effort to evaluate.

nature-econ-675.q: Why is bid rigging harmful to the seller in an auction?
nature-econ-675.a: It weakens competition, discourages other bidders and denies the seller the item's true value.

nature-econ-705.q: What is a crowding game, and what is a congestion game?
nature-econ-705.a: In a crowding game each player's payoff falls as more others choose the same strategy, as when extra cars slow a road for everyone; a congestion game is a crowding game in networks.

nature-econ-681.q: In the hawk–dove game, what do V and C stand for, and which is assumed to be larger?
nature-econ-681.a: V is the value of the resource and C is the cost of an escalated fight; the cost is almost always assumed larger than the value.

nature-econ-692.q: In a Bayesian game, how do players form their beliefs about the unknown state of nature?

nature-econ-733.q: What does Kuhn's theorem show about mixed and behavior strategies?
nature-econ-733.a: The two are equivalent in finite extensive-form games with perfect recall, where players remember all past actions.

nature-econ-710.q: How does kin selection explain altruism, and what does Hamilton's rule say?
nature-econ-710.a: Kin selection explains it through shared genes; Hamilton's rule says relatedness must exceed the ratio of cost to benefit.

nature-econ-740.q: When does reciprocal altruism work, in terms of cost and gain?
nature-econ-740.a: It works where the cost to the helper of sharing food, mates, nests or territory is less than the gain to the one helped.

nature-econ-726.q: Who introduced the Shapley value, and when?

nature-econ-696.q: In cooperative game theory, when does one allocation dominate another?
nature-econ-696.a: When some coalition prefers it and could obtain at least its members' payoffs on its own.

nature-econ-429.q: How is the derivative of a function defined formally?
nature-econ-429.a: It is the limit of the ratio of change in output to change in input as the input change shrinks to zero.

nature-econ-427.q: When is a twice-differentiable function of one variable convex?
nature-econ-427.a: Exactly when its second derivative is never negative.

nature-econ-474.q: What defines a steady state in continuous time and in discrete time?
nature-econ-474.a: In continuous time the rate of change of each property is zero; in discrete time each period-to-period difference is zero.

nature-econ-436.q: What are difference equations also called, and what are they the counterpart of?
nature-econ-436.a: They are also called recurrence relations, and are the discrete-time counterpart of differential equations.

nature-econ-445.q: How can a growth rate be estimated from data over time using logarithms?
nature-econ-445.a: By running a linear regression of log x on time.

nature-econ-211.q: In Bayesian updating, what is a prior distribution?
nature-econ-211.a: It is the belief about a parameter before any data are seen, which is turned into posterior probabilities.

nature-econ-453.q: In complementary slackness, picturing the solution as a particle, when can a constraint push back?
nature-econ-453.a: Only when the particle touches the constraint's boundary.
